screens.title: Introduction to IP Addressing and Subnetting
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn why every device needs a unique IPv4 address and how subnetting defines which devices share the same network. IPv4 is a 32-bit label usually shown as four decimal octets like 192.168.1.10. Those 32 bits split into a network portion and a host portion, and the subnet mask tells us where the split happens. We use bitwise operations — most commonly a bitwise AND between an IP and its mask — to calculate the network address. You will practice converting octets between binary and decimal, learn how to derive the broadcast address by setting host bits to one, and identify usable host ranges between network and broadcast addresses. We also cover CIDR notation, the concise way to state how many bits are network bits. A practical outcome: after this lesson you can take an IP plus mask, compute network ID, broadcast, and the first and last usable hosts. A common beginner mistake is assigning the network or broadcast address to a host; we'll highlight why those addresses are reserved and how that breaks connectivity. Consider this your map for speaking in binary and reading network boundaries with confidence.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These first four objectives focus on the essential skills you need to reason about IPv4 networks. First, you will explain the structure of an IPv4 address, recognizing octets and how they form the 32-bit label. Knowing this structure matters because it lets you translate between human-readable dotted-decimal and the underlying binary that routers use. For example, converting 192.168.1.10 into binary shows how each octet maps to eight bits. Second, you will convert between binary and decimal for both addresses and masks. Practicing conversions helps you determine network boundaries by inspection. Third, you'll learn the purpose of a subnet mask and how it defines network and host portions; the mask is a sequence of ones followed by zeros that marks which bits identify the network. Finally, you will identify, for a given IP and mask, the network address, the broadcast address, and the usable host range. This skill prevents common mistakes like assigning reserved addresses. Each objective is paired with a small mnemonic to help you visualize bits, and a verified competency milestone signals readiness to practice with live address examples.

screens.title: IPv4 Structure and Octets
screens.narratorSegment: An IPv4 address is a 32-bit number usually shown in dotted-decimal form: four octets separated by dots, like 192.168.1.10. Each octet is eight bits long and can represent any number from 0 to 255. Understanding octets matters because subnet masks and common network math work across these 8-bit boundaries, and many learners mentally group addresses by octet when planning networks. Concretely, converting 192.168.1.10 to binary yields four 8-bit groups; reading those groups is how you visualize which bits fall into the network portion when a mask is applied. A typical misconception is to think each decimal octet independently defines a network or host—rather, the mask determines which bits across octets are network bits. For example, a /24 mask (255.255.255.0) makes the first three octets network bits and the last octet host bits. But a /26 mask can split host bits inside the last octet, producing subnet boundaries that do not align with whole octets in human-readable terms. Takeaway: practice splitting an IP into four octets, convert each to binary, and count ones when you read a mask. This daily habit will make later bitwise operations and subnet calculations intuitive.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › IPv4 Structure
IPv4 Structure and Octets
Four octets, each 8 bits, form the 32-bit address you will convert and mask.
Definition & Explanation
An octet is eight bits. Grouping four octets produces the human-readable dotted-decimal format. Practice converting octets to binary to see bit patterns.
Decimal
192 . 168 . 1 . 10
Binary
11000000 . 10101000 . 00000001 . 00001010
Common misconception
Treating octets as fixed network/host boundaries. Masks can cross octet boundaries and create subnets inside an octet.
Concrete example and practice
Convert each octet of 192.168.1.10 to binary by subtracting powers of two. Verify the binary groups map back to the decimal values. This is the first step before applying a subnet mask.
Example
192 → 128+64 = 11000000; 10 → 8+2 = 00001010. Practicing this builds fluency for subnet math.
Key Takeaway

Read addresses as four octets, convert each octet to binary, and count bits when you later apply masks.

screens.title: Subnet Masks: Purpose and Binary Form
screens.narratorSegment: A subnet mask is a 32-bit number that distinguishes which bits of an IPv4 address identify the network and which identify hosts. In binary a mask is a contiguous block of ones followed by zeros. The ones mark the network portion; the zeros mark the host portion. For example, 255.255.255.0 becomes 11111111.11111111.11111111.00000000. That mask declares the first 24 bits as network bits and leaves the final eight bits for host addresses. Understanding masks in binary is essential because masks like 255.255.255.192 (binary ending with 11000000) create subnets that do not align to whole octets. A common mistake is to read masks only as dotted-decimal without visualizing the bit pattern; this leads to errors when the mask is non-standard. Practice converting masks to binary, count the ones to produce the CIDR length, and learn the decimal values that correspond to partial octet masks (128, 192, 224, 240, 248, 252, 254). This practice helps you quickly identify subnet sizes and the number of host bits available. Question to reflect on: when you see a mask with 26 ones, how many host bits remain and what does that mean for usable addresses?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Subnet Masks
Subnet Masks: Purpose and Binary Form
Masks mark network bits with ones and host bits with zeros; converting to binary reveals where the split occurs.
Mask binary patterns
Common masks and their binary equivalents help you recognize partial-octet splits quickly.
255.255.255.0 → 11111111.11111111.11111111.00000000 (/24)
255.255.255.192 → 11111111.11111111.11111111.11000000 (/26)
255.255.255.240 → 11111111.11111111.11111111.11110000 (/28)
Common misconception
Assuming masks always align to octet boundaries; many useful subnets use bits inside an octet and must be counted in binary.
Concrete practice and takeaway
To get comfortable, convert a mask to binary and count ones to find CIDR. Then calculate the number of host bits: 32 minus the CIDR length, and compute host capacity as 2^host_bits - 2 for usable addresses in typical networks.
Key Takeaway

Convert masks to binary, count ones to obtain /prefix length, and use the remaining host bits to estimate usable addresses.

screens.title: Deriving the Network Address (Bitwise AND)
screens.narratorSegment: Deriving a network address uses a simple, repeatable process: convert IP and mask to binary, apply a bitwise AND between corresponding bits, then convert the resulting binary back to dotted-decimal. The bitwise AND preserves network bits and clears host bits because AND with one keeps a bit, AND with zero clears it. For example, take 192.168.1.10 and mask 255.255.255.0. Convert both into four binary octets, then AND each pair; the first three octets remain because the mask bits are ones, and the last octet becomes zero because the mask bits are zeros, yielding network 192.168.1.0. A common beginner error is doing decimal subtraction or arithmetic instead of bitwise logic; this produces incorrect networks. Follow this three-step routine for every calculation: binary conversion, bitwise AND, and decimal conversion back. Practice this on masks that split inside an octet — you'll see how the AND operation clears only the host bits and leaves network bits intact. Final reflection: can you perform the AND mentally for a /26 mask and an IP within that block? Deriving the Network Address (Bitwise AND) means convert both ip and mask to binary, and them bit-by-bit, then convert the result back to dotted-decimal to get the network address.. In practical terms, step-by-step: convert, and, and interpret the result. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Convert both IP and mask to binary, AND them bit-by-bit, then convert the result back to dotted-decimal to get the network address.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Network Address
Deriving the Network Address (Bitwise AND)
A repeatable three-step procedure to compute the network ID from any IP/mask pair.
Process steps
  1. Convert IP and mask to binary octets.
  2. Apply bitwise AND across each corresponding bit pair.
  3. Convert the resulting binary octets back to dotted-decimal.
Example walk-through
IP: 192.168.1.10 → 11000000.10101000.00000001.00001010
Mask: 255.255.255.0 → 11111111.11111111.11111111.00000000
AND → 11000000.10101000.00000001.00000000 → 192.168.1.0
Pitfall & practice
Don't subtract decimals or borrow across octets; always operate on bits. Practice with a /26 mask where only the first two bits of the last octet are network bits to see partial-octet AND behavior.
Key Takeaway

Use the convert → AND → convert routine for every network calculation to avoid common arithmetic mistakes.

screens.title: Broadcast Address and Usable Host Range
screens.narratorSegment: A broadcast address is the highest address in a subnet and is used to send packets to all hosts in that subnet. To compute it, take the network address and set every host bit to one. For a network 192.168.1.0/24, where host bits are the final eight bits, the broadcast is 192.168.1.255. Usable hosts are the addresses between the network address and the broadcast address — specifically, network plus one through broadcast minus one. These two extremes are reserved and cannot be assigned to individual devices. A frequent beginner error is attempting to assign the network or broadcast address to a host, causing addressing conflicts and unreachable devices. Another important point: when masks are non-octet-aligned, the broadcast calculation still sets only the host bits to one, which may change only part of an octet. Practice computing the first and last usable addresses for subnets like /26 and /27 to internalize how subnet size affects usable capacity. Reflection: how does a /30 subnet change usable hosts compared to a /24, and why might a /30 be used for point-to-point links? Broadcast Address and Usable Host Range means broadcast = network with host bits set to one; usable hosts exclude network and broadcast addresses and fall between those two values.. In practical terms, how to compute the broadcast and which addresses are assignable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Broadcast vs usable
keyIdea.text: Broadcast = network with host bits set to one; usable hosts exclude network and broadcast addresses and fall between those two values.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Broadcast & Hosts
Broadcast Address and Usable Host Range
Compute broadcast by setting host bits to one; usable hosts exclude network and broadcast addresses.
How to compute broadcast
Start from network address and set all host bits to one. Convert binary to decimal to obtain dotted-decimal broadcast.
Network: 192.168.1.0 (/24) → Host bits 00000000 → set to 11111111 → Broadcast: 192.168.1.255
Usable host range
First usable = network + 1. Last usable = broadcast - 1. In /24 example: .1 through .254.
Example: /26 subnet
A /26 mask leaves 6 host bits. If the network is 192.168.1.0/26, the broadcast is 192.168.1.63 and usable hosts are .1 through .62. Blocks increment by 64 in the last octet: 0–63, 64–127, etc.
Key Takeaway

Always reserve network and broadcast addresses; compute usable range as network+1 to broadcast-1, regardless of mask boundary alignment.

screens.title: CIDR Notation and Why It Replaced Classes
screens.narratorSegment: CIDR notation writes an IP network as an address followed by a slash and the number of network bits, for example 192.168.1.0/24. This compact form replaces classful thinking by explicitly stating how many bits are network bits, regardless of historical A/B/C classes. You should be able to translate between /prefix lengths and dotted-decimal masks: /24 = 255.255.255.0, /26 = 255.255.255.192, and so on. The prefix length directly tells you how many host bits remain (32 minus the prefix) and therefore how many usable addresses the subnet supports. A common misconception is to assume /24 always maps to a class C or that classes constrain addressing; CIDR allows flexible, efficient subnetting across the IPv4 space. Practically, CIDR is used in configuration and routing tables because it simplifies aggregation and route advertisement. When planning subnets, convert the slash length to host bits, calculate 2^host_bits minus two for usable hosts, and ensure the block aligns with the desired increment. Try converting /27 and /30 to see why /30 is used for point-to-point links with only two usable hosts. CIDR Notation and Why It Replaced Classes means cidr uses a slash and a number to show the count of network bits; convert it to dotted-decimal and compute host capacity from remaining bits.. In practical terms, slash notation explained and how it maps to masks and subnet sizes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › CIDR Notation
CIDR Notation and Why It Replaced Classes
Express masks succinctly with a slash and prefix length; compute host bits from the prefix.
Quick mapping
/24 → 255.255.255.0 → host bits = 8 → usable = 254
/26 → 255.255.255.192 → host bits = 6 → usable = 62
/30 → 255.255.255.252 → host bits = 2 → usable = 2
Practical note
CIDR simplifies route aggregation and avoids the rigidity of classful addressing. Use it in configuration and planning for clarity and precision.
Concrete example
Given 192.168.5.65/27, convert /27 to mask 255.255.255.224, find block size 32 in last octet, identify subnet 192.168.5.64–192.168.5.95 and broadcast .95.
Key Takeaway

Use CIDR to state network length quickly; convert the prefix to host bits to decide subnet size and usable host counts.

screens.title: Configuring an Interface on a Cisco Router
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring an IP on an interface is a practical step where addressing knowledge meets device configuration. On a Cisco router you enter interface configuration mode, assign the IP and subnet mask, and bring the interface up. The commands follow a consistent pattern: interface selection, ip address declaration with dotted-decimal mask, no shutdown, and then exit. After configuration you verify with commands that display the interface address and status. Understanding this flow matters because a correctly applied address and mask is required for routing and for the device to participate in a network. An example from the chapter shows how to assign 192.168.1.1 with a 255.255.255.0 mask to GigabitEthernet0/1 and then verify. A common mistake is entering the wrong mask or forgetting no shutdown, which leaves the interface administratively down despite a correct address. Practice these commands, then confirm the address appears in the interface listing to ensure the device is configured and reachable. How would you verify a different interface if the initial show output doesn't list it? Configuring an Interface on a Cisco Router means use interface, ip address, and no shutdown commands, then verify with show commands to confirm correct ip and mask application.. In practical terms, cli commands to apply an ip and verify the interface. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Binary ↔ Decimal Conversion Practice
screens.narratorSegment: Converting between binary and decimal is a core practical skill. For an octet, list the powers of two: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. To convert decimal to binary, subtract the largest power you can and mark a one, then continue with the remainder. To convert binary to decimal, sum the powers of two where there is a one. For example, convert the octet 192 to binary by subtracting 128 and 64 leaving zero, so binary is 11000000. Conversely, binary 00001010 sums 8 and 2 to yield decimal 10. A useful classroom routine is to write the power row, place ones and zeros beneath, and quickly sum columns where ones appear. Beginners often forget to keep eight columns in each octet and produce inconsistent lengths. Always pad to eight bits per octet when writing binary to prevent alignment errors when applying masks. Practice this routine across several octets and masks until it feels mechanical; this fluency makes later tasks like performing bitwise AND or deriving broadcast addresses fast and accurate. In practical terms, step practice converting masks and addresses reliably. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Worked Example: 172.16.10.50 with 255.255.255.192
screens.narratorSegment: Let's work the provided hands-on scenario step by step: IP 172.16.10.50 with mask 255.255.255.192. First, convert the relevant octet where the mask applies — the mask ends with 192 which in binary is 11000000, so the first two bits of the last octet are network bits and the last six are host bits. Convert the IP's last octet, 50, to binary: 50 = 32 + 16 + 2 → 00110010. Now apply the mask: AND 00110010 with 11000000 gives 00000000 for the last octet, so the network's last octet is 0. The network address becomes 172.16.10.0. To get the broadcast, set the six host bits to one: last octet becomes 00111111 which is decimal 63, yielding broadcast 172.16.10.63. Usable hosts run from 172.16.10.1 through 172.16.10.62. Common confusion occurs when learners forget to apply the mask only where it has zeros and ones; always perform the AND bit-by-bit. Final check: how many usable hosts does this subnet provide? With six host bits you have 2^6 - 2 = 62 usable addresses. Worked Example: 172.16.10.50 with 255.255.255.192 means apply binary conversion and bitwise and to compute network 172.16.10.0, broadcast 172.16.10.63, usable hosts .1 through .62 for a /26 block.. In practical terms, follow the binary steps to find network, broadcast, and usable range. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Worked Example: 172.16.10.50 with 255.255.255.192
Binary conversion, AND operation, and final host range for a /26 subnet.
Step-by-step
Mask last octet 192 → 11000000 (/26). IP last octet 50 → 00110010. AND: 00110010 & 11000000 = 00000000 → network last octet 0.
Results
Network: 172.16.10.0
Broadcast: 172.16.10.63
Usable: 172.16.10.1 – 172.16.10.62

This calculation identifies the specific segment a server belongs to and which addresses can be assigned safely. Mistaking the block boundaries can lead to overlap and routing issues.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Common mistakes in addressing are easy to make but simple to catch with a checklist. One frequent error is assigning the network or broadcast address to a host — these addresses are reserved and cause connectivity problems. Another is using an incorrect mask, for example typing 255.255.255.0 when the network requires /26; this misplaces the host into the wrong subnet block. Learners also sometimes forget to pad binary octets to eight bits, misaligning masks during AND operations. In configuration, forgetting no shutdown or applying the mask to the wrong interface are operational mistakes that appear unrelated to addressing but prevent communication. A recommended troubleshooting flow: verify the configured IP and mask, compute the network and broadcast to confirm the host falls inside the usable range, verify the interface state, and then check routing adjacency if necessary. Practicing the checklist with sample IP/mask pairs makes both calculation and operational verification routine. Final reflective question: when next you see a misbehaving device, which of these checks will you run first and why? screens.narratorSegment: Practicing targeted questions helps solidify your reasoning. Consider this sample: given IP 10.0.0.130 with mask 255.255.255.240, which network contains the address? The mask 255.255.255.240 is /28, leaving 4 host bits and a block size of 16 in the last octet. The fourth octet of 130 falls in the 128–143 block, so the network is 10.0.0.128. Work the bitwise AND if you need confirmation. Another sample asks for the broadcast when given 192.168.5.65/27. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn why every device needs a unique IPv4 address and how subnetting defines which devices share the same network. IPv4 is a 32-bit label usually shown as four decimal octets like 192.168.1.10. Those 32 bits split into a network portion and a host portion, and the subnet mask tells us where the split happens. We use bitwise operations — most commonly a bitwise AND between an IP and its mask — to calculate the network address. You will practice converting octets between binary and decimal, learn how to derive the broadcast address by setting host bits to one, and identify usable host ranges between network and broadcast addresses. We also cover CIDR notation, the concise way to state how many bits are network bits. A practical outcome: after this lesson you can take an IP plus mask, compute network ID, broadcast, and the first and last usable hosts. A common beginner mistake is assigning the network or broadcast address to a host; we'll highlight why those addresses are reserved and how that breaks connectivity. Consider this your map for speaking in binary and reading network boundaries with confidence.

These first four objectives focus on the essential skills you need to reason about IPv4 networks. First, you will explain the structure of an IPv4 address, recognizing octets and how they form the 32-bit label. Knowing this structure matters because it lets you translate between human-readable dotted-decimal and the underlying binary that routers use. For example, converting 192.168.1.10 into binary shows how each octet maps to eight bits. Second, you will convert between binary and decimal for both addresses and masks. Practicing conversions helps you determine network boundaries by inspection. Third, you'll learn the purpose of a subnet mask and how it defines network and host portions; the mask is a sequence of ones followed by zeros that marks which bits identify the network. Finally, you will identify, for a given IP and mask, the network address, the broadcast address, and the usable host range. This skill prevents common mistakes like assigning reserved addresses. Each objective is paired with a small mnemonic to help you visualize bits, and a verified competency milestone signals readiness to practice with live address examples.

The second objectives expand conversion practice and introduce CIDR. First, you will deepen your binary-to-decimal fluency for subnet masks so you can interpret non-octet boundaries like a /26 or /27 mask. This matters when you design subnets that are smaller than legacy classful networks. Second, you will use CIDR notation to express mask length compactly; writing 192.168.1.0/24 is shorter and clearer than a dotted-decimal mask and it is the standard in modern configuration. Third, you will practice bitwise operations to derive the network address from an IP and mask, and then compute the broadcast by setting all host bits to ones. Fourth, you'll apply these skills to practical scenarios and CLI configuration checks on Cisco devices, learning to verify with the ip address command and show ip interface brief. Each card includes a small visual mnemonic or timeline to help you remember process steps, and a milestone marker to confirm readiness to perform live calculations.

An IPv4 address is a 32-bit number usually shown in dotted-decimal form: four octets separated by dots, like 192.168.1.10. Each octet is eight bits long and can represent any number from 0 to 255. Understanding octets matters because subnet masks and common network math work across these 8-bit boundaries, and many learners mentally group addresses by octet when planning networks. Concretely, converting 192.168.1.10 to binary yields four 8-bit groups; reading those groups is how you visualize which bits fall into the network portion when a mask is applied. A typical misconception is to think each decimal octet independently defines a network or host—rather, the mask determines which bits across octets are network bits. For example, a /24 mask (255.255.255.0) makes the first three octets network bits and the last octet host bits. But a /26 mask can split host bits inside the last octet, producing subnet boundaries that do not align with whole octets in human-readable terms. Takeaway: practice splitting an IP into four octets, convert each to binary, and count ones when you read a mask. This daily habit will make later bitwise operations and subnet calculations intuitive.

A subnet mask is a 32-bit number that distinguishes which bits of an IPv4 address identify the network and which identify hosts. In binary a mask is a contiguous block of ones followed by zeros. The ones mark the network portion; the zeros mark the host portion. For example, 255.255.255.0 becomes 11111111.11111111.11111111.00000000. That mask declares the first 24 bits as network bits and leaves the final eight bits for host addresses. Understanding masks in binary is essential because masks like 255.255.255.192 (binary ending with 11000000) create subnets that do not align to whole octets. A common mistake is to read masks only as dotted-decimal without visualizing the bit pattern; this leads to errors when the mask is non-standard. Practice converting masks to binary, count the ones to produce the CIDR length, and learn the decimal values that correspond to partial octet masks (128, 192, 224, 240, 248, 252, 254). This practice helps you quickly identify subnet sizes and the number of host bits available. Question to reflect on: when you see a mask with 26 ones, how many host bits remain and what does that mean for usable addresses?

Deriving a network address uses a simple, repeatable process: convert IP and mask to binary, apply a bitwise AND between corresponding bits, then convert the resulting binary back to dotted-decimal. The bitwise AND preserves network bits and clears host bits because AND with one keeps a bit, AND with zero clears it. For example, take 192.168.1.10 and mask 255.255.255.0. Convert both into four binary octets, then AND each pair; the first three octets remain because the mask bits are ones, and the last octet becomes zero because the mask bits are zeros, yielding network 192.168.1.0. A common beginner error is doing decimal subtraction or arithmetic instead of bitwise logic; this produces incorrect networks. Follow this three-step routine for every calculation: binary conversion, bitwise AND, and decimal conversion back. Practice this on masks that split inside an octet — you'll see how the AND operation clears only the host bits and leaves network bits intact. Final reflection: can you perform the AND mentally for a /26 mask and an IP within that block? Deriving the Network Address (Bitwise AND) means convert both ip and mask to binary, and them bit-by-bit, then convert the result back to dotted-decimal to get the network address.. In practical terms, step-by-step: convert, and, and interpret the result. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A broadcast address is the highest address in a subnet and is used to send packets to all hosts in that subnet. To compute it, take the network address and set every host bit to one. For a network 192.168.1.0/24, where host bits are the final eight bits, the broadcast is 192.168.1.255. Usable hosts are the addresses between the network address and the broadcast address — specifically, network plus one through broadcast minus one. These two extremes are reserved and cannot be assigned to individual devices. A frequent beginner error is attempting to assign the network or broadcast address to a host, causing addressing conflicts and unreachable devices. Another important point: when masks are non-octet-aligned, the broadcast calculation still sets only the host bits to one, which may change only part of an octet. Practice computing the first and last usable addresses for subnets like /26 and /27 to internalize how subnet size affects usable capacity. Reflection: how does a /30 subnet change usable hosts compared to a /24, and why might a /30 be used for point-to-point links? Broadcast Address and Usable Host Range means broadcast = network with host bits set to one; usable hosts exclude network and broadcast addresses and fall between those two values.. In practical terms, how to compute the broadcast and which addresses are assignable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Converting between binary and decimal is a core practical skill. For an octet, list the powers of two: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. To convert decimal to binary, subtract the largest power you can and mark a one, then continue with the remainder. To convert binary to decimal, sum the powers of two where there is a one. For example, convert the octet 192 to binary by subtracting 128 and 64 leaving zero, so binary is 11000000. Conversely, binary 00001010 sums 8 and 2 to yield decimal 10. A useful classroom routine is to write the power row, place ones and zeros beneath, and quickly sum columns where ones appear. Common mistakes in addressing are easy to make but simple to catch with a checklist. One frequent error is assigning the network or broadcast address to a host — these addresses are reserved and cause connectivity problems. Another is using an incorrect mask, for example typing 255.255.255.0 when the network requires /26; this misplaces the host into the wrong subnet block. Learners also sometimes forget to pad binary octets to eight bits, misaligning masks during AND operations. These are the core concepts to carry forward. First, an IPv4 address is 32 bits split into four octets; practice converting octets to binary until it becomes second nature. Second, a subnet mask is a 32-bit number of contiguous ones then zeros; the ones mark the network portion and zeros mark hosts. Third, CIDR notation is a compact way to state how many network bits are used, for example /24. Remember that computing the network uses a bitwise AND, and computing the broadcast sets host bits to one; addresses between them are the usable hosts. Keep a simple checklist for troubleshooting: verify the configured IP and mask, compute network and broadcast to confirm the host falls into the usable range, check interface state, then verify routing.
